about: The committed matrix of docs/upstream-parity.md (decision D6): each cell holds an image of wz to the original built by this repository, with the verdict of decision D1 (WIN, TIE or LOSS; only WIN counts). The rows of a run are the output of `scripts/lib/kit_compare.py --format rows` for that run, never figures copied by hand; a change that moves a cell moves its run here, in the same commit, with the run that measured it.

runs.target: mcu-zephyr: the T2G kit (CYT4BF, Cortex-M7 at 350 MHz) on its own Ethernet to a zenohd 1.10.0 with its REST plugin on the bench host
runs.workload: W1: answer the two GETs of the wz client's keys, 2,000 times each per boot, through the router
runs.method: scripts/kit-lane.sh compare --boots 12, compare builds (CONFIG_WZ_MEMORY_REPORT), images alternated per round, turnaround read at the host's wire
runs.reference: zephyr-pico-queryable-st: zenoh-pico with the wz client's planes (queryable, UDP unicast) in its single-threaded arm, the stronger of its two arms in every cell of this run
runs.tree: origin's main at 417232b694 with the SCE pin at dc579571aa (ADR 0076: a machine's internal queue is sized by the depth the generator proves from its document, 0 for both of the client's, and its external queue by `sce:capacity`, 2 for the session machine) and zenoh-pico at 1.10.2 as the reference (its text reads 8 bytes more than at 1.10.1); the kernel heap pools of both images stated by the quarter-free rule: the wz heap client 11,264 bytes, zenoh-pico 13,312 in both arms; sent to the bench host
caveats: Two programs written for one workload, the same keys, bodies and encoding on the wire (decision D4): the cells move to pico's own programs on both libraries when the pico C ABI runs on the MCU (step M5).

The ram cell holds each image's static RAM, which includes its kernel heap pool. Both pools are stated by the rule HW.7 holds a main stack to, a quarter free (peak * 4 <= pool * 3): the wz heap client 11,264 bytes (it ran with 9,216, the least tried, at its heap peak of 8,412 then) and zenoh-pico 13,312 in both arms (the single-threaded arm answered with 9,728 and did not answer with 9,216; both searches were made at zenoh-pico 1.10.1, and the twelve boots of this run ran at 1.10.2 with these pools; the multi-threaded arm's least was not searched). Both pools were 131,072 until the run before. The fixed client takes nothing from the heap and has none.

Both sides of this run poll the receive path out of the ITCM (CONFIG_WZ_POLL_PATH_IN_ITCM). The turnaround of the fixed client reads 0.1889 ms against 0.1996 for the single-threaded pico, ratio 0.9468 (interval 0.9292 to 0.9673, twelve boots of each image): WIN. The heap client reads 0.1971, ratio 0.9875 (interval 0.9478 to 1.0097): TIE, where the two runs before read WIN (0.9624 and 0.9491). The heap client and the fixed client are one code but for where the storage block is, and the difference of their medians has changed sign between the three runs (+0.5, -2.3 and +8.1 microseconds, heap minus fixed): it was not examined, and the cell is graded as this run reads it.

The text cells are of the compare builds, which carry the memory report: the fixed client reads 143,620 bytes here and 142,528 in the build the kit lane's text gate holds (deploy/text_budget.json), 1,092 more; the heap client 143,552 against 142,452, 1,100 more. The reference reads 144,844 bytes.

The stack_used cell is the difference of two sums of thread readings, and only the difference is the cell's. Both wz clients read 5,652 against 5,692, 40 bytes (0.7 percent) under; the main thread of each reads 2,720 (the receive of a handshake message, not a query's answer). The fixed client read 5,668 in a run before, its receive queue thread of the network stack reading 512 where the runs after read 496; that thread is Zephyr's, and why its reading differs between runs of one code was not examined.

The heap_peak cell of the heap client is its storage block, 8,224 bytes, taken from the kernel heap at start, and the allocator's own 28: 8,252 bytes against the reference's 9,280. The block was 11,568 bytes before the batch, the reply limit, the queues and the delayed-send queues of the two machines were stated by what the client carries (a batch of 1,024 bytes and replies of 96 are this firmware's numbers: the documents it answers with are 63 and 72 bytes, and a router takes the smaller of its batch and the node's).

The margins are small: text 1,224 bytes (0.85 percent) for the fixed client and 1,292 (0.89) for the heap client, flash 1,320 and 1,388, stack_used 40 bytes for both, ram 9,077 (7.9 percent) and 6,597 (5.7), and the fixed client's turnaround interval ends 3.3 percent under 1. Text and flash are of deterministic builds, so they hold until a change moves them; a change is read against these margins and not against the verdict.

The text and the instruction-cache layout move together on this kit: the same source read 41.4 and 42.0 us in the stamps with 392 bytes of unreached code between them, so a turnaround difference below a microsecond is not attributed to a source change.
